chunks: "The lost power turns into heat in the pass transistor.
The LDO's input current is basically the output current, so the power wasted is (V in-V out) times I out , plus a small V in times I Q for the regulator's own quiescent current.
For 5 volts to 3. 3 volts at 500 milliamps that's 0. 85 watts, about half of the 1. 65 watts the load receives. That heat has to get out of the chip.
It flows from the junction to the package, to the PCB copper and out to the air.
The temperature rise is power times thermal resistance: with 60 degrees Celsius/W the junction sits 51 degrees Celsius above ambient.
So at 70 degrees Celsius ambient it's about 121 degrees Celsius, close to a typical 125 degrees Celsius rating.
If it gets past the limit, the part's thermal shutdown turns it off, then it cools and tries again, so you get an output that pulses or drops out.
To deal with it I'd reduce the headroom, because the power is proportional to V in-V out : put a buck in front, tap a lower rail, or even drop some voltage in a series resistor off-chip.
Or improve the thermal path with copper area, thermal vias and a package with an exposed pad. Or derate the current.
And at some point the answer is that this should be a buck converter."
